subject: maths
title: Line Graphs and Data: Change over Time and the Mode
seo_title: Year 5 Line Graphs and Data Worksheets: Change over Time, Mode and Dot Plots (Free, with Answer Key)
standard_text: Interpret line graphs representing change over time; discuss the relationships that are represented and conclusions that can be made
meta_desc: Free Year 5 maths worksheets on line graphs and data for the Australian Curriculum: read scales, find rises and falls over time, compare two lines, find the mode in dot plots and column graphs, and decide which conclusions the data supports. 100 NAPLAN-style questions with an answer key.
key_big: Check the scale first. Then look for where the line rises, falls or stays flat.
key_sub: Work out what one small square is worth and where the scale starts. The steepest part shows the biggest change. The mode is the value that appears most often. A conclusion must be shown by the data.
body_html:
Read a line graph

A line graph shows how something changes over time. Time goes along the bottom. First check the scale: count the small squares between two labels and work out what one square is worth. Also check where the scale starts. It does not always start at 0.

To read a value, go up from the time to the dot, then across to the scale.

Example 1

How much did the temperature rise from 6 am to 2 pm?

6 am: 14 °C. 2 pm: 25 °C. Rise = 25 − 14 = 11.

Answer: 11 °C

Rises, falls and flat parts

A line going up shows an increase. A line going down shows a decrease. A flat line shows no change. The steepest part shows the fastest change. It is not always next to the highest point.

Example 2

Between which two readings did the temperature rise the most?

8 am to 10 am: 19 − 16 = 3. 10 am to 12 pm: 23 − 19 = 4. 12 pm to 2 pm: 25 − 23 = 2. The biggest rise is 4 °C.

Answer: 10 am to 12 pm

When a graph has two lines, use the key to see which line is which. “How much warmer” or “how many more” means find the difference: subtract.

The mode and the shape of data

In a dot plot, each dot is one piece of data. The mode is the value that appears most often: the tallest stack. In a column graph, the mode is the category with the tallest column.

Example 3

What is the mode?

The tallest stack has 7 dots, above 2. The mode is the value 2, not the number of dots (7) and not the biggest value (8).

Answer: 2 books

To describe the shape, say where most of the data is, and point out any gaps or values far away from the rest.

Kinds of data

Kind of dataWhat the answers areExample
Nominal categoricalCategories with no orderFavourite sport, eye colour
Ordinal categoricalCategories with an orderShirt size S, M, L; never, sometimes, always
NumericalNumbers you count or measureNumber of pets, height in cm

Is the conclusion supported?

A conclusion is supported only if the graph shows it. A graph of one day cannot tell you about every day, and a survey of one class cannot tell you about all of Australia. If the graph does not show something, such as rain, you cannot say it from the graph.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting each small square as 1Work out the scale: 2 squares between 0 and 20 means 10 each
Reading the scale as if it starts at 0Check the first label: the scale may start at 20
Reading the graph at the wrong timeGo straight up from the time on the bottom axis
Choosing the highest point for the biggest riseFind the steepest part and subtract
Giving the highest value or the number of dots as the modeThe mode is the value with the most dots
Making a conclusion the data does not showCheck that the graph really shows it

faq.q: What do Year 5 students learn about data in the Australian Curriculum?
faq.a: In Year 5 students interpret line graphs that show change over time and discuss what conclusions can be made. They also collect and show nominal, ordinal and numerical data, and describe it using the mode and the shape of the data.

faq.q: How do you read a line graph?
faq.a: Check what each small square on the scale is worth and where the scale starts. Then go up from the time on the bottom axis to the line, and across to the scale.

faq.q: What is the mode in maths?
faq.a: The mode is the value or category that appears most often. In a dot plot it is the tallest stack of dots, and in a column graph it is the tallest column.

faq.q: What is the difference between nominal and ordinal data?
faq.a: Both are categorical data. Nominal categories have no order, such as favourite sport, while ordinal categories have an order, such as shirt sizes S, M, L.

items.q: What is each small square on the temperature scale worth?
items.e: The labels go 20, 25, 30, 35. There are 5 small squares between two labels. 5 ÷ 5 = 1, so each small square is 1 °C.

items.q: What was the temperature at 8 am?
items.e: Go up from 8 am to the dot, then across. It is 3 small squares above 20, so 23 °C. (3 °C forgets that the scale starts at 20, not 0.)

items.q: What was the temperature at 12 pm?
items.e: At 12 pm the dot is on the labelled line for 30, so 30 °C. (31 °C is the reading at 2 pm.)

items.q: What was the highest temperature?
items.e: The highest dot is at 2 pm. It is 1 small square above 30, so 31 °C. (35 °C is the top of the scale, not a reading.)

items.q: The temperature was measured every 2 hours. At which time did it read 28 °C?
items.e: Find 28 on the scale (3 small squares above 25). The dot on that line is at 4 pm.

items.q: What was the lowest temperature?
items.e: The lowest dot is at 6 am: 1 small square above 20, so 21 °C. (20 °C is the bottom of the scale, and 26 °C is the reading at 6 pm, not 6 am.)

items.q: What is each small square on the water scale worth?
items.e: The labels go up in 1000s. There are 2 small squares between two labels, so each square is 1000 ÷ 2 = 500 L.

items.q: How much water was in the tank on Tuesday?
items.e: Go up from Tue to the dot. It is on the line halfway between 3000 and 4000, so 3500 L.

items.q: How much water was in the tank on Friday?
items.e: Each small square is 500 L. On Friday the dot is halfway between the lines for 4000 and 4500. Halfway between them is 4250 L.

items.q: On which day were there 3750 L of water in the tank?
items.e: 3750 L is halfway between 3500 and 4000. The dot halfway between those lines is above Sat, so Saturday.

items.q: What was the most water in the tank during the week?
items.e: The highest dot is on Thursday, on the line halfway between 4000 and 5000: 4500 L. (5000 L is the top of the scale, not a reading.)

items.q: What is each small square on the height scale worth?
items.e: The labels go up in 20s. There are 2 small squares between two labels, so each square is 20 ÷ 2 = 10 cm.

items.q: How tall was the sunflower in week 2?
items.e: In week 2 the dot is halfway between the lines for 30 and 40, so 35 cm. (20 cm is week 1.)

items.q: How tall was the sunflower in week 4?
items.e: In week 4 the dot is on the labelled line for 80, so 80 cm. (8 cm counts each small square as 1 cm.)

items.q: In which week did the sunflower first reach 1 metre (100 cm)?
items.e: Find 100 on the scale. The first dot on that line is in week 5. (In week 4 it was only 80 cm.)

items.q: How tall was the sunflower when it was first measured, in week 0?
items.e: Week 0 is the first dot. It is on the first small line above 0, so 10 cm. (The sunflower was already 10 cm tall, not 0 cm.)

items.q: What is each small square on the scale for people worth?
items.e: The labels go up in 50s. There are 2 small squares between two labels, so each square is 50 ÷ 2 = 25 people.

items.q: How many people were at the beach at 10 am?
items.e: At 10 am the dot is halfway between the lines for 100 and 150. Halfway is 125.

items.q: How many people were at the beach at 2 pm?
items.e: At 2 pm the dot is halfway between 250 and 300, so 275. (225 people is the 12 pm reading.)

items.q: A lifeguard counted the people every 2 hours. At which count were there 200 people?
items.e: Find 200 on the scale. The dot on that line is at 4 pm. (At 12 pm there were 225 people.)

sets.title: Change over time: rises, falls and flat parts

items.q: By how much did the temperature rise from 6 am to 2 pm?
items.e: 6 am: 21 °C. 2 pm: 31 °C. Rise = 31 − 21 = 10 °C. (8 is the number of hours, not degrees.)

items.q: Between which two readings did the temperature rise the most?
items.e: Find the steepest part going up. 8 am to 10 am: 27 − 23 = 4 °C. 10 am to 12 pm: 3 °C. 12 pm to 2 pm: only 1 °C, even though 2 pm is the highest point.

items.q: Between which two readings did the temperature fall the most?
items.e: The line goes down after 2 pm. 2 pm to 4 pm: 31 − 28 = 3 °C. 4 pm to 6 pm: 28 − 26 = 2 °C. So it fell most from 2 pm to 4 pm.

items.q: How much did the temperature fall from 2 pm to 6 pm?
items.e: 2 pm: 31 °C. 6 pm: 26 °C. Fall = 31 − 26 = 5 °C. (3 °C is only the first 2 hours.)

items.q: After which reading did the temperature start to fall?
items.e: The line goes up until the dot at 2 pm (31 °C). After 2 pm it goes down.

items.q: Between which two days did the amount of water go up?
items.e: The line goes up only once: from Wednesday (3000 L) to Thursday (4500 L). Everywhere else it goes down.

items.q: By how much did the water go up from Wednesday to Thursday?
items.e: Thursday 4500 L − Wednesday 3000 L = 1500 L. (3 is the number of small squares; each square is 500 L.)

items.q: How much water was used from Monday to Wednesday?
items.e: Monday 4000 L, Wednesday 3000 L. 4000 − 3000 = 1000 L. (500 L is only one day.)

items.q: From Friday to Sunday the line falls by the same amount each day. How much water was used each day?
items.e: Friday 4250 L, Saturday 3750 L, Sunday 3250 L. Each day it fell by 500 L. (1000 L is the total for 2 days.)

items.q: What does the rise from Wednesday to Thursday most likely show?
c: Rain added water to the tank
The family used a lot of water
items.e: Using water makes the line go down. The line goes up, so water was added to the tank, most likely by rain.

items.q: How much mass did the puppy gain from 2 months to 8 months?
items.e: 2 months: 3 kg. 8 months: 12 kg. Gain = 12 − 3 = 9 kg. (6 is the number of months.)

items.q: Between which two ages did the puppy gain the most mass?
items.e: Find the steepest part. 3 to 4 months: 8 − 5 = 3 kg. Every other step is 2 kg or less. (At 7 and 8 months the puppy is heaviest, but it is not gaining mass.)

items.q: Between which two ages did the puppy’s mass stay the same?
items.e: A flat line shows no change. From 7 to 8 months the line stays on 12 kg.

items.q: What does the flat part of the line at the end show?
c: The puppy’s mass did not change
items.e: A flat line means the value stays the same: 12 kg at 7 months and at 8 months. The graph does not tell us anything about eating.

items.q: Between which two counts did the number of people go up the most?
items.e: 10 am to 12 pm: 225 − 125 = 100 people. 8 am to 10 am: 75. 12 pm to 2 pm: 50. The steepest rise is 10 am to 12 pm, not the part that reaches the highest point.

items.q: Between which two counts did the number of people go down the most?
items.e: 2 pm to 4 pm: 275 − 200 = 75 fewer. 4 pm to 6 pm: 200 − 75 = 125 fewer. So 4 pm to 6 pm.

items.q: How many more people were at the beach at 2 pm than at 8 am?
items.e: 2 pm: 275. 8 am: 50. How many more means subtract: 275 − 50 = 225. (9 is the number of small squares; each one is 25 people.)

items.q: Between which two weeks did the sunflower grow the most?
items.e: Find the steepest part. Week 3 to week 4: 80 − 55 = 25 cm. Week 4 to 5: 20 cm. Week 5 to 6: only 10 cm, even though week 6 is the tallest.

items.q: How much did the sunflower grow from week 4 to week 6?
items.e: Week 4: 80 cm. Week 6: 110 cm. 110 − 80 = 30 cm.

items.q: From week 5 to week 6 the line is less steep than before. What does that show?
items.e: The line still goes up, so it kept growing (100 cm to 110 cm). Less steep means it grew less that week: 10 cm instead of 20 cm.

sets.title: Compare two lines on one graph

items.q: Use the key. What was the temperature in Melbourne at 10 am?
items.e: Melbourne is the dashed line with squares. Each small square is 2 °C. At 10 am it is on the labelled line for 10, so 10 °C. (28 °C is Darwin.)

items.q: What was the temperature in Darwin at 2 pm?
items.e: Darwin is the solid line with dots. At 2 pm the dot is 1 small square above 30. Each small square is 2 °C, so 30 + 2 = 32 °C.

items.q: How much warmer was Darwin than Melbourne at 2 pm?
items.e: 2 pm: Darwin 32 °C, Melbourne 14 °C. How much warmer means subtract: 32 − 14 = 18 °C. (9 is the number of small squares between the lines; each is 2 °C.)

items.q: By how much did the temperature in Melbourne rise from 6 am to 2 pm?
items.e: Melbourne (dashed): 6 am 6 °C, 2 pm 14 °C. 14 − 6 = 8 °C. (12 °C is the rise in Darwin.)

items.q: At what time were both cities at their warmest?
items.e: The highest point of each line is at 2 pm: Darwin 32 °C and Melbourne 14 °C.

items.q: How much warmer was Darwin than Melbourne at 6 am?
items.e: 6 am: Darwin 20 °C, Melbourne 6 °C. 20 − 6 = 14 °C.

items.q: Was Melbourne’s highest temperature lower than Darwin’s lowest temperature?
items.e: Melbourne’s highest was 14 °C (2 pm). Darwin’s lowest was 20 °C (6 am). 14 is lower than 20, so the whole Melbourne line is below the Darwin line.

items.q: How tall was Kai’s sunflower in week 2?
items.e: Kai is the dashed line. In week 2 it is on the line for 40, so 40 cm. (35 cm is Mia’s.)

items.q: How tall was Kai’s sunflower in week 6?
items.e: Week 6, dashed line: halfway between 110 and 120, so 115 cm. (110 cm is Mia’s.)

items.q: In which week were the two sunflowers the same height?
items.e: Look for the place where the two lines meet. In week 3 both are 55 cm.

items.q: Whose sunflower was taller in week 5, and by how much?
items.e: Week 5: Mia 100 cm, Kai 85 cm. Mia’s is taller: 100 − 85 = 15 cm.

items.q: In how many of the weeks was Kai’s sunflower taller than Mia’s?
items.e: The dashed Kai line is above the solid line in weeks 0, 1, 2 and 6. In week 3 they are the same, so it does not count.

items.q: In which week was the difference between the two heights the biggest?
items.e: Find the biggest gap between the lines. Week 5: 15 cm. Week 1 and week 4: 10 cm. Week 6: 5 cm. (Week 6 has the tallest sunflower, not the biggest gap.)

items.q: How many books did 5B borrow in week 3?
items.e: 5B is the dashed line. The scale starts at 20 and each small square is 2 books. In week 3 the square marker is 2 small squares above 30, so 34. (14 forgets that the scale starts at 20.)

items.q: How many books did the two classes borrow altogether in week 5?
items.e: Week 5: 5A 42, 5B 30. Altogether means add: 42 + 30 = 72.

items.q: How many more books did 5B borrow than 5A in week 6?
items.e: Week 6: 5B 44, 5A 38. How many more means subtract: 44 − 38 = 6.

items.q: In which week did both classes borrow the same number of books?
items.e: The two lines meet in week 4. Both classes borrowed 36 books.

items.q: Between which two weeks did 5B’s borrowing fall the most?
items.e: Use the dashed 5B line. It goes down twice: week 1 to 2 (30 − 26 = 4) and week 4 to 5 (36 − 30 = 6). So week 4 to week 5. (Week 5 to 6 is the biggest change, but it is a rise.)

items.q: Which class borrowed more books in the 6 weeks altogether?
In which week was the difference between the classes the biggest?
items.e: Week 5: 42 − 30 = 12 books. In weeks 1, 3 and 6 the gap is 6. (Week 6 has the highest point, but the gap is only 44 − 38 = 6.)

sets.title: Mode and the shape of data

items.q: Each dot is one student. What is the mode of the data?
items.e: The mode is the value that appears most often: the tallest stack of dots. 9 students have 1 pet, so the mode is 1 pet. (9 is how many students, and 6 is the highest value, not the mode.)

items.q: How many students have 2 pets?
items.e: Count the dots above 2: there are 6. Each dot is one student.

items.q: How many students are in 5C?
items.e: Each dot is one student, so count all the dots: 4 + 9 + 6 + 3 + 1 + 1 = 24. (40 is the total number of pets, not students.)

items.q: How many students have no pets?
items.e: No pets is the value 0. There are 4 dots above 0.

items.q: Which sentence best describes the shape of the data?
c: The dots are spread out evenly
Most students have 4 or more pets
items.e: 4 + 9 + 6 = 19 of the 24 students have 0, 1 or 2 pets. Most of the dots are on the left, and only a few are on the right.

items.q: One value is far away from the rest of the data. Which value is it?
items.e: The dot at 6 is on its own, with a gap at 5. All the other dots are between 0 and 4.

items.q: Each dot is one swimmer. What is the mode of the data?
items.e: The tallest stack of dots is above 6, so the mode is 6 laps. (7 is how many swimmers swam 6 laps, and 12 is the highest value.)

items.q: How many swimmers swam more than 6 laps?
items.e: More than 6 means 7, 8 or 12 laps: 5 + 2 + 1 = 8 swimmers. Do not count the swimmers who swam exactly 6.

items.q: Which numbers of laps did nobody swim?
items.e: There are no dots above 9, 10 and 11. This is a gap in the data. 3 and 12 each have one dot.

items.q: Which sentence best describes the shape of the data?
c: Every swimmer swam a different number of laps
The swimmers are spread out evenly
items.e: 4 + 7 + 5 = 16 of the 22 swimmers swam 5, 6 or 7 laps. The dots are bunched in the middle, with one far away at 12.

items.q: What is the mode of this data?
items.e: The mode is the category chosen most often: the tallest column. That is Netball. The mode is the sport, not the number 9.

items.q: How many students chose AFL?
items.e: The scale is labelled in 2s, with a grid line for every 1. The AFL column ends on the line between 6 and 8, so 7.

items.q: What kind of data is “favourite sport”?
items.e: The answers are names of sports, so the data is categorical. The sports have no natural order, so it is nominal.

items.q: What is the mode of the shirt sizes?
items.e: The tallest column is M, so the mode is size M. (12 is how many students, and XL is the biggest size, not the most common one.)

items.q: Shirt size is ordinal categorical data. What does ordinal mean here?
c: The sizes have an order: S, M, L, XL
Each size has a different colour
items.e: Ordinal data is in categories that have a natural order. S is smaller than M, M is smaller than L, and so on.

items.q: Which of these is numerical data?
c: The number of pets at home
items.e: Numerical data is counted or measured, so the answers are numbers. Favourite fruit and eye colour are nominal. Shirt size is ordinal.

items.q: Which of these is ordinal categorical data?
items.e: Never, sometimes, often, always are categories with an order. Colours and pets have no order (nominal). Number of brothers and sisters is numerical.

items.q: What is the mode of the family sizes?
items.e: The tallest column is above 4, so the mode is 4 people. (10 is how many families, and 6 is the biggest family.)

items.q: Which sentence best describes the shape of the data?
c: There are the same number of each size
items.e: 6 + 10 + 5 = 21 of the 26 families have 3, 4 or 5 people. The columns are tallest in the middle and short at each end.

items.q: A new student with 3 pets joins 5C. What is the mode now?
items.e: Add one dot above 3: now 4 students have 3 pets. The tallest stack is still above 1 (9 dots), so the mode is still 1 pet.

items.q: Which statement is supported by the graph?
c: It is 31 °C at 2 pm every day
It was warmer at 4 pm than at 10 am
items.e: 4 pm: 28 °C. 10 am: 27 °C. So 4 pm was warmer. The graph shows one day only, so it cannot tell us about every day. It does not show rain. 6 pm (26 °C) was warmer than 6 am (21 °C).

items.q: Which statement is supported by the graph?
c: It will rain again next Thursday
The family used 500 L every day
There was more water on Thursday than on Monday
The tank was empty on Wednesday
items.e: Thursday: 4500 L. Monday: 4000 L. The water did not fall by 500 L every day (Thursday to Friday it fell 250 L). The graph cannot tell us about next week. On Wednesday there were still 3000 L.

items.q: After Sunday the family keeps using 500 L each day, and it does not rain. How much water will be in the tank on Tuesday?
The tank can hold 5000 L. How much more water could it hold on Thursday?
items.e: On Thursday it held 4500 L. 5000 − 4500 = 500 L more would fill it.

items.q: Kai says, “My sunflower grew more than Mia’s, because it is taller in week 6.” Is he right?
items.e: Mia: 110 − 10 = 100 cm. Kai: 115 − 15 = 100 cm. They grew the same amount. Kai’s started taller, so it finished taller. (115 cm and 110 cm are heights, not growth.)

items.q: Isla says, “Darwin was 18 °C warmer than Melbourne all day.” Is this supported?
c: Yes: at 2 pm it was 18 °C warmer
No: Melbourne was warmer at 6 pm
Yes: the lines are always the same distance apart
No: at 6 am it was only 14 °C warmer
items.e: At 2 pm the difference was 32 − 14 = 18 °C, but at 6 am it was 20 − 6 = 14 °C. One time is not enough to say “all day”.

items.q: From 2 pm to 6 pm, which city’s temperature fell more?
items.e: Darwin: 32 − 26 = 6 °C. Melbourne: 14 − 10 = 4 °C. 6 is more than 4, so Darwin fell more. (26 °C is the 6 pm reading, not the fall.)

items.q: Which statement is supported by the dot plot?
c: Students with more pets are happier
More students have 1 pet than any other number
Half the class has no pets
items.e: 1 pet has the tallest stack (9 dots). Only 4 of the 24 students have no pets, which is not half. The dot plot does not tell us how happy anyone is.

items.q: Which statement is supported by the graph?
c: The beach was busiest at 2 pm
There are 275 people at 2 pm every Saturday
The beach was busiest at 6 pm
It rained at 6 pm, so people went home
items.e: The highest point is at 2 pm (275 people). The graph does not show the weather, and it is one Saturday only, so it cannot tell us about every Saturday.

items.q: The surf club wants 1 lifeguard on duty for every 50 people at the beach (or part of 50). How many lifeguards are needed at 2 pm?
items.e: At 2 pm there were 275 people. 5 lifeguards cover 5 × 50 = 250 people. 25 people are left over, so 1 more is needed: 6 lifeguards.

items.q: Jack goes for a swim when the temperature is 30 °C or more. At which readings was it 30 °C or more?
items.e: 12 pm: 30 °C and 2 pm: 31 °C. 30 °C counts, because it says 30 °C or more. 4 pm (28 °C) and 10 am (27 °C) are below 30.

items.q: Lachlan’s puppy weighed 3 kg at 2 months. At what age did it first weigh more than 3 times as much?
items.e: 3 × 3 kg = 9 kg. At 4 months it was 8 kg, which is not more than 9 kg. At 5 months it was 10 kg, so 5 months.

items.q: Mia’s sunflower keeps growing the same amount each week as it did from week 5 to week 6. How tall will it be in week 8?
items.e: From week 5 to week 6 it grew 110 − 100 = 10 cm. Two more weeks: 110 + 10 + 10 = 130 cm.

items.q: Swimmers who swam 8 laps or more can join the relay team for the swimming carnival. How many swimmers is that?
items.e: 8 laps or more means 8 and 12 (nobody swam 9, 10 or 11). 2 + 1 = 3 swimmers.

items.q: How many more students chose netball than cricket?
items.e: Netball: 9. Cricket: 4. How many more means subtract: 9 − 4 = 5.

items.q: A student says, “Netball is the most popular sport in Australia.” Is this supported by the graph?
c: No: the survey is of one class only
No: AFL has the tallest column
Yes: netball has the tallest column
items.e: The graph shows the favourite sport in 5D only. One class cannot tell us about the whole of Australia.

items.q: Size M shirts come in packs of 5. How many packs must the school order so every student who needs size M gets one?
items.e: 12 students need size M. 2 packs give 10 shirts, which is not enough. 3 packs give 15 shirts, so order 3 packs.

items.q: How many families have more than 4 people?
items.e: More than 4 means 5 or 6 people: 5 + 2 = 7 families. Families with exactly 4 people do not count.

items.q: Which question can you answer using this graph?
c: How old is each person in the families?
What is the most common family size in 5E?
How many families in Perth have 4 people?
items.e: The graph shows how many people are in each family in 5E. So it can tell us the most common size (the mode). It does not show ages, pets or other places.

items.q: The librarian gives a class a prize in any week it borrows 40 books or more. How many prizes were given in the 6 weeks?
items.e: 5A borrowed 42 books in week 5, and 5B borrowed 44 books in week 6. Every other point is below 40. So 2 prizes.
